After a ceasefire last month, it sent in bulldozers to demolish more buildings, saying it was targeting Hezbollah infrastructure.M FARAH: This is the church. And this is the part that was completely destroyed a couple of days ago. Completely wiped out.ARRAF: It's risky, even for people in neighboring villages, to take video of Yaroun. So residents have pooled their money to try to get high-resolution satellite images from commercial providers.M FARAH: Either somebody - each time someone will buy it or we get to have the...(SOUNDBITE OF CELLPHONE RINGING)M FARAH: ...Funds in a certain account and try to buy.ARRAF: Each image they obtain costs at least $112. In Mazen Farah's apartment in Beirut, his 75-year-old father, Hanna Farah, has only a photo of his former home, with its terracotta roof and roses in the garden.HANNA FARAH: (Speaking Arabic).ARRAF: "We worked hard to build the house and raise our children," he says. Mazen Farah said he had security cameras running constantly around the house. None showed any fighters. Geryes Saloum, a municipality employee, built a three-bedroom home in Yaroun 10 years ago. On the day we meet him at Farah's house, his home was still standing, according to the images, but all the houses around it were destroyed.GERYES SALOUM: (Through interpreter) Every day, I wait for a picture to arrive from Yaroun. I mean, when Mazen's house was destroyed three days ago, I didn't sleep.ARRAF: Many of the properties in Yaroun and other villages are owned by American citizens, Lebanese who left during Israel's 18-year-long occupation of south Lebanon in the '80s and '90s. In upstate New York, Hanna Hanna saw from a satellite image that his 92-year-old mother's house had been razed.HANNA HANNA: Oh, our house has gone because we saw it being demolished in the first satellite image. There's nothing there. It's just rubble.ARRAF: He says they expected it to happen, but still...H HANNA: You know, it's - you get this image. You see it for the first time, and your heart sinks, you know?ARRAF: The next image they saw showed two more houses destroyed - and this...H HANNA: We can still see the bulldozer in the image. On the left of the image, the last image we received, we can see the bulldozer still there.ARRAF: He says the house he had just started building was also demolished, including a $30,000 stone wall. His brother Naoum Hanna, his partner in an upstate New York construction company, says he spent more than $470,000 he and his wife worked for years to earn on a house they plan to retire to.NAOUM HANNA: We confirmed yesterday through a blurry image - satellite image - that we know it's gone.ARRAF: His brother Hanna says, as an American, the use of tax dollars to fund the Israeli military is a bitter pill to swallow.H HANNA: Those are properties of American taxpayers who are very active in America, who work hard, pay their dues. And American bombs and American bulldozers destroyed them.ARRAF: He says no one spends money on their dream home and then uses it to store weapons. Some spent much more. We reached Qasem Fares in Panama.QASEM FARES: (Speaking Arabic).ARRAF: He's 68. He left southern Lebanon, essentially penniless, at the age of 15, making a fortune in Central America. He spent more than $10 million on a house in Bint Jbeil, near Yaroun, where he spent summers with his children and grandchildren. Twelve bedrooms, a huge swimming pool, a cinema, gyms - proof he had made good. All of it gone.FARES: (Speaking Arabic).ARRAF: "My son sent me the picture and told me what happened," he says. "I cried all day when I saw it."Jane Arraf, NPR News, Beirut. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. articles.full_content: Transcript DEBBIE ELLIOTT, HOST: Celebrations broke out today in India after the country's education minister resigned. It was a major victory for India's so-called cockroach movement, which had spurred hundreds of thousands of Gen Zers to take to the streets, and posed the most serious challenge in years to the Hindu nationalist BJP government. NPR's Omkar Khandekar spoke to the protesters and revelers in New Delhi.OMKAR KHANDEKAR, BYLINE: It was a moment they were waiting for for weeks. And as India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, posted his resignation letter on X...(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: We have done it. We have done it.(CHEERING)KHANDEKAR: ...Tens of thousands in New Delhi hugged and cheered and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)UNIDENTIFIED MUSICAL ARTIST: (Singing in non-English language).KHANDEKAR: Pradhan's resignation followed a seven-week sit-in by the Cockroach Janta Party, an online satire that became a political force with millions of followers among India's Gen Z. They hold him responsible for leaked questions on exams for university slots or government jobs that millions of students take each year. Students were asked to retake the exams.(SOUNDBITE OF POLICE SIRENS WAILING)UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: (Non-English language spoken).UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: (Non-English language spoken).UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #4: (Non-English language spoken).KHANDEKAR: Delhi police attacked demonstrators with batons and tear gas earlier this week. That spawned similar protests across a dozen Indian cities. Social media flooded with memes and reels mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A popular slogan was...(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)UNIDENTIFIED GROUP: (Chanting in non-English language).UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #5: (Chanting in non-English language).UNIDENTIFIED GROUP: (Chanting in non-English language).UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #5: (Chanting in non-English language).KHANDEKAR: ...Whenever Modi is scared, he brings out the cops. Trainee doctor Mohit Dhaka, whose face was covered in a celebratory pink powder today, said the news of the minister's resignation feels surreal.MOHIT DHAKA: People are congratulating each other. I don't know, some random person is hugging me. Some random people are just lifting me up, and everything is like - it's more than a family.KHANDEKAR: Taka, who studies in Hyderabad, was among many who traveled hundreds of miles to join the protest in the Indian capital. They slept on pavements and railway stations. People across the country sent them food and water through delivery apps. Dhaka said the movement was India's spirit at its best.DHAKA: This is one of the landmark events in my life. This will shape my future. This will shape the future of a lot of people who are here.KHANDEKAR: The Cockroach Party leaders have now called off the strike, but they have also sought compensation for students who died by suicide from the stress of having to retake the leaked exams and punishment for the police who attacked the protesters. Political scientist Milan Vaishnav says the protesters succeeded because the government's usual playbook of undermining or intimidating its critics failed.MILAN VAISHNAV: This set of protesters was very difficult for the government to take on because the people who made up the protests - these young, urban, aspirational Indians - have been part of the BJP's core demographic.KHANDEKAR: So, he says, the government appeared to want to cut its losses by cutting loose the education minister. Neha, a political science student at today's celebration, says the past few weeks were about experiencing democracy in action. She shared only her first name, saying she did not want to be profiled by her caste surname.NEHA: This is my right. This is your right. This is our right to ask accountability to them, who think they are superior but not superior more than constitution, right?KHANDEKAR: And she hopes that the protest would serve as a reminder that power flows from the people, not a cabinet post. Omkar Khandekar, NPR News, New Delhi. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. David Ramos/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption David Ramos/Getty Images Perhaps you saw the ecstatic scenes this week of Spain's World Cup Championship team arriving back home after they won the tournament in a thrilling 1- zero — excuse me, it's soccer — one - nil victory over Argentina. La Roja, as they've become known for their red jerseys, took off from Newark airport, landed in Madrid and rode in an open-topped red bus emblazoned "STARS SHINE TOGETHER", to be acclaimed by an estimated 2 million fans, shouting, cheering, and sobbing, as the team hoisted the FIFA World Cup trophy. You may wonder: what fuels great athletes to play 120 minutes against their mightiest competitors, win by a single goal, and then fly through the night across the Atlantic to parade before their grateful nation? Sponsor Message Love of country? Love of the game? Or pizza from West Orange, New Jersey? Shortly after Spain secured their victory, the phone trilled at Bagels by Jarrett, or BXJ, which also call themselves, "The most confused bagel shop you've ever loved." The owner, Jarrett Seltzer, and his crew also make pizza, and had made a stack of them for Norway's World Cup team after they defeated Brazil in the Round of 16. "I guess they don't have a lot of pizza in Norway," Jarrett Selzer told us. Maybe when the world's best soccer players flop to the ground in theatrical pain to try and draw fouls, they whisper to each other, "Pssst: Try the pizza at BXJ," because on Norway's apparent recommendation, the Spanish team ordered 46 pies: pepperoni, margherita, and buffalo chicken. "And a few gluten free," Seltzer told us. He also said he had been restlessly experimenting for months to perfect his recipe for pizza dough. "To go from good to better," he said. "But hard work really does pay off," he told us. "To feed the guys who just won the World Cup? I don't know if there's a cooler feeling. "You try and do something as good as you can, and get better and better, and then just one day, it all pays off," Jarrett Seltzer said. "Like it did for us and those guys on the team. They're always eating such healthy diets. What's a better way to say, 'Finally, we won!' than a big New Jersey pizza?"

articles.full_content: Transcript AILSA CHANG, HOST: President Trump's tariffs have caused an array of problems for him. They have raised prices. Polls show voters don't like the tariffs. And they have caused other countries to retaliate. The Supreme Court ruled in February against some of Trump's most sweeping tariffs, and yet Trump has kept tariffs as a cornerstone of his economic agenda. In fact, after that Supreme Court ruling, he vowed to find a way to revive his tariffs.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: But other alternatives will now be used to replace the ones that the court incorrectly rejected. We have alternatives, great alternatives.CHANG: Well, then last night, Trump announced a new wave of tariffs, hitting 59 countries and the European Union. Here to tell us more about all of this are NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben and NPR senior business editor Rafael Nam. Hello to both of you.DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Hey there.RAFAEL NAM, BYLINE: Hey.CHANG: Hey. OK, Danielle, I want to start with you. Can you just tell us more about these newest tariffs? Like, what are they replacing exactly?KURTZLEBEN: Right, so these new tariffs have two tiers, 10% and 12.5%, and they cover all of the biggest U.S. trading partners, which are responsible for almost all of the imports to the U.S. Now, that said, some major categories of goods are exempted here, like energy and some types of foods.CHANG: OK.KURTZLEBEN: Now, these new tariffs will replace a temporary global 10% blanket tariff that Trump put into place right after that Supreme Court decision you mentioned. That tariff expired this week. These new tariffs took their place. Now, to impose these new tariffs, the administration is using a law intended to counter other countries', quote, "unfair trade practices." In this case, the U.S. is accusing all of its major trading partners of not doing enough to fight the use of forced labor. Now, not everyone buys that rationale. Democratic representative Richard Neal from Massachusetts said in a statement that Trump is just hunting for legal justifications, and that the new tariffs are, quote, "too convenient to be taken seriously."CHANG: And wait, these weren't even the only tariffs that Trump imposed this week, right?KURTZLEBEN: Right. He also announced new tariffs on some specific categories of Canadian goods. Those are 50% tariffs, so they're pretty high.CHANG: Yeah.KURTZLEBEN: And they're set to take effect in just under a month. The administration said those are to retaliate against Canada's own retaliation against U.S. tariffs last year.CHANG: Back and forth, back and forth. OK, but we're in this time when the cost of living - it's such a top concern for so many households. How do you think these tariffs will affect those households?NAM: The good news - if you can call it that - is that they're not significantly higher than the tariffs they are replacing. But they are still a lot higher than they were at the start of the second Trump administration. And this has a real impact on American families, especially at a time, like you said, Ailsa, when the cost of living is a real concern. It's also that the war with Iran has led to a big increase in gas prices. The Budget Lab at Yale University says the latest tariffs will add a little under a percentage point to consumer inflation. And in dollar terms, that means an additional tax of $1,100 to households per year, essentially.CHANG: Wow.NAM: All of this clearly has a knock-on effect, according to Natasha Sarin, the president of the Budget Lab. Inflation rises because of tariffs, people therefore spend less, and the end result is a hit to the economy. This is how she put it.NATASHA SARIN: You never make up that. It's sort of a permanent decline in the economy's strength as a result of this type of policy.NAM: And that's why many economists think tariffs are a really bad idea.CHANG: Well, given that tariffs are adding to people's financial problems, why go through with them?KURTZLEBEN: Well, this White House has a couple of policy reasons. First, they often use tariffs as leverage to get concessions from other countries on trade agreements, and it's possible, by the way, that that could happen with these new Canada tariffs I mentioned. Like I said, there's almost a month until they go into effect, and the U.S. and Canada still need to sit down and renegotiate the USMCA trade pact. So these tariffs could change or disappear during those negotiations.CHANG: OK.KURTZLEBEN: Now, the White House's main rationale for tariffs is that they will revitalize manufacturing. That boom has not materialized yet in jobs. In fact, there are fewer manufacturing jobs now than when Trump took office. Now, the White House has also claimed trillions of dollars in new investment as a result of trade deals stemming from his tariffs. New investment could result in more jobs, but also the numbers have been unclear and we still have to see when or if all of that money materializes.CHANG: Exactly. OK, so Rafael, the administration is saying tariffs will pay off. But we're obviously living in the present moment. What kind of effects are these tariffs having right now?NAM: So besides the higher cost of living, the main thing is that it does make things unpredictable. Take the Federal Reserve. Tariffs are just another complication at a time when policymakers are grappling with higher energy costs and high borrowing costs. For example, the average 30-year mortgage just hit its highest in nearly a year. All of this could make it more likely the Fed will have to raise interest rates this year, which goes against the president that ` has been arguing that the Fed should be lowering rates.But for businesses today, the effects of these tariffs are real. You've heard us say this time and time again. Businesses hate uncertainty, and right now, that's what they're getting. Not only that, the president has a habit of threatening to impose additional tariffs all of a sudden. He did that with Canada earlier this week, for example.CHANG: Right.NAM: And Sarin at the Budget Lab says those kinds of sudden actions make life extremely tough for businesses.SARIN: And so I think that makes it, like, really challenging from the perspective of businesses who are trying to plan to understand, like, what their costs are going to be, and also then what prices they're going to have to charge consumers for these goods if you don't have any real sense of the ways in which the policy is evolving.NAM: So Trump may be arguing tariffs will pay off, but businesses, though, are not feeling it right now.CHANG: But OK, Danielle, just make this make sense. Like, how do these tariffs make sense politically with midterm elections approaching?KURTZLEBEN: Well that's really a gamble, I think. Trump's pro tariff argument is essentially, I'm using these now to make great deals. They can bring in some revenue, but the biggest economic effects will show up eventually. Now, some voters may buy into that long-term narrative, but polls have shown that tariffs have grown less and less popular and that, along with higher gas prices from the Iran War, has dragged the president's approval down. Now, if you're a Republican running this November, you have a tough question. Do you try to create daylight between yourself and Trump on tariffs? And if you do, how do voters react, and how does the president react? Both of those things are very unpredictable.CHANG: That is NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben and Rafael Nam. Thank you to both of you.KURTZLEBEN: Yeah, thank you.NAM: Thank you. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. articles.title: Democrats in Maine formally nominate Troy Jackson as their new U.S. Senate candidate
articles.summary: Troy Jackson speaks during Maine Democrats' nominating convention at the Bangor Cross Insurance Center on Saturday in Bangor, Maine. Ashley L. Conti for NPR hide caption
articles.full_content: Troy Jackson speaks during Maine Democrats' nominating convention at the Bangor Cross Insurance Center on Saturday in Bangor, Maine. Ashley L. Conti for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ashley L. Conti for NPR BANGOR, Maine — Democrats in Maine have officially selected Troy Jackson as their new nominee for U.S. Senate. He will face longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins in what will be one of the most closely watched races in this fall's midterm election. Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, emerged victorious at a nominating convention held by the state party in Bangor, Maine, on Saturday. He won his party's nod with the support of 566 of 571 delegates who voted at the convention. "They will say that a grassroots campaign, powered by working people, cannot defeat Susan Collins and every powerful interest standing behind her. They are wrong again," Jackson said in an acceptance speech. "Because we can, we can together. Shoulder to shoulder, we can defeat Susan Collins, and we can take back that Senate seat, and we can build a government that finally works for working Mainers, not the power brokers who write the biggest checks anymore." Sponsor Message Jackson replaces Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee. Platner suspended his campaign earlier this month after a woman he once dated came forward and accused him of raping her in 2021. Platner has denied the allegation, but it was the final straw for Democrats after months of controversy surrounding him. Now, after an abbreviated and chaotic search for a replacement, Maine Democrats are looking to move past Platner's scandal-plagued campaign and rally behind Jackson, hoping he can harness the same energy and momentum. Jackson did not mention Platner by name in his remarks. But he sought to reach out to his supporters, saying he has always known "that your trust has to be earned." Jackson interacts with delegates after being nominated as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. Ashley L. Conti for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ashley L. Conti for NPR "I want you to hear this directly from me: there is a place in this campaign for all of you. There is work for you in this movement," he said. The Senate race in Maine holds far-reaching political implications. Democrats need to net a total of four seats to win back control of the chamber this fall, and party officials see the contest in Maine as one of their best opportunities to gain ground. Maintaining Platner's movement, without the controversy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from northern Maine, is running on an economic populist message that mirrors much of what Platner emphasized in his campaign, rejecting the Democratic establishment and focusing on affordability concerns, backing policies like Medicare for All and raising taxes on the ultra-wealthy and large corporations. Sponsor Message Like other more progressive candidates on the left, Jackson is pushing for the abolishment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and an end to U.S. military aid to Israel. He's also advocating for Congress to pass civil rights legislation protecting LGBTQ Americans and federalize the right to an abortion — two issues where he's changed his views after taking more conservative stances during his early years in public office. When asked about Jackson's history with reproductive rights, Democratic state Sen. Stacy Brenner argued that it wasn't a deterrent in supporting him. "What I find compelling about legislators and policymakers is when they are able to evolve with the thinking of where their heart is, where their mind is, when they learn about data and when they hear stories [from] their constituents," said Brenner, who also has a background as a farmer and nurse. "That's what's happened for Troy," she added. Jackson supporters celebrate his lengthy tenure in Maine politics as well as his blue-collar roots. And despite recent reporting in The Washington Post and CNN describing Jackson as exhibiting a short temper with colleagues during his time in office, he has faced minimal public pushback from state leaders in the lead-up to the convention. Delegates cheer for Jackson after he secured his party's nomination for Senate. Ashley L. Conti for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ashley L. Conti for NPR Delegates from all 16 Maine counties participated in Saturday's nominating convention. Ashley L. Conti for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ashley L. Conti for NPR "He's passionate. He doesn't deviate. He's funny. He can get a little testy at times because he's passionate," said former state Sen. Susan Deschambault as she walked into the Cross Insurance Center where the convention was taking place Saturday. "That's what we need. We don't like what's going on now." Whether Jackson can command the same level of enthusiasm that Platner garnered over the past year remains an open question, even to some Mainers who plan to cast their ballot for Jackson this fall. Some Democrats contend that Platner and Jackson share the same set of values when it comes to the issues, arguing that is what will keep the momentum going for the party heading into the general election. Sponsor Message "Troy Jackson has been working at getting these progressive policies in Maine for years, like since before I was born," said 22-year-old delegate Kaia De Vries, a graduate student at the University of Maine. "It wasn't [Platner's] movement. This is a progressive movement that still exists, that will continue without him being a public-facing part of it." Standing next to De Vries, 30-year-old Aurora Green agreed, saying no one individual is the face of this moment. "This isn't about Graham Platner. This isn't even about Troy Jackson," she said. "This is about a movement of working-class Mainers and workers coming together and saying that we aren't going to be bought out and that we deserve better." A tough road ahead for the nominee While Collins has faced competitive challengers before, Democrats see the fifth-term incumbent as particularly vulnerable this year. She's running in a state carried by Kamala Harris in 2024, and at a moment when many voters have soured on President Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, walks in the annual Moxie Day Parade on July 11 in Lisbon, Maine. Scott Eisen/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption Scott Eisen/Getty Images Still, Jackson will face a difficult path to victory, with only about 100 days before voting ends on Nov. 3 to build up a war chest and make his case to voters. In a statement for the Collins campaign, spokesperson Shawn Roderick criticized Jackson for what he described as a "partisan record of driving up costs, hurting our schools, and making life less affordable for families across the state." "Senator Collins looks forward to waging a vigorous and issues-oriented campaign that will distinguish her record of accomplishment against Troy's angry sound bites and far-left ideology," the campaign said. In Collins, Jackson is running against one of the most senior Republican incumbents in the Senate. Collins, who has held her seat for 30 years, holds a massive fundraising edge, reporting $11 million in cash on hand, according to latest Federal Election Commission filings. "We can build a government that finally works for working Mainers," Jackson told delegates during his acceptance speech on Saturday. Ashley L. Conti for NPR hide caption toggle caption Ashley L. Conti for NPR But Jackson's campaign argues that it has momentum, reporting a fundraising haul of more than $1 million since he announced his run. Sponsor Message Jackson concluded his remarks Saturday with a call for unity. "If you believe our freedoms are worth defending, stand with us. And if you believe that Maine deserves a senator who will fight like hell for working class people, well stand with us," he said. "We have a party to unite, we have a movement to build, and we have a senator to defeat, and together, we are going to win."

articles.full_content: Transcript DEBBIE ELLIOTT, HOST: Less than three weeks after Graham Platner ended his bid for the U.S. Senate, Democrats in Maine have officially selected a replacement - Troy Jackson.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TROY JACKSON: If you believe that Maine deserves a senator who will fight like hell for working-class people, well, stand with us.ELLIOTT: He's a former Maine state Senate president and won the vast majority of delegates at the party convention in Bangor today. Jackson will face off against longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins this fall in what's expected to be one of the most competitive Senate races in the country. NPR political reporter Elena Moore was at the convention and joins us now to talk about it, Hi there, Elena.ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Hi.ELLIOTT: So let's start with a quick recap of why this happened.MOORE: Well, because Democrats needed a new candidate, and fast. Their initial nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out earlier this month after a woman he previously dated came forward and accused him of raping her. He denies the allegation, but it was the final straw after a string of scandals for Platner. So to fill his spot, Maine Democrats held the convention. They gathered nearly 600 delegates and put it to a vote. It wasn't close. Jackson won all but five delegates. And that was no surprise because nearly all of his primary rivals had already dropped out.ELLIOTT: How is it that Democrats coalesced around Jackson so quickly?MOORE: Well, he's no stranger to Maine politics, spending two decades in state government, and he's built a record advocating for a handful of issues that were really core to Platner's campaign, too, like passing Medicare for All and raising taxes on corporations and the ultra-wealthy.Plus, Jackson has a blue-collar background. He's a fifth-generation logger. And at a time when a lot of voters say they're struggling to keep up with high costs and feel like leaders in D.C. aren't listening to them, voters see Jackson as a better advocate for rural and working-class Mainers.ELLIOTT: OK, so he swept at the convention with the party faithful, but will Jackson be able to rally the rank-and-file voters who were so enthusiastic about Platner?MOORE: Yeah, in conversations I've had, folks who supported Platner are now backing Jackson. But for some, watching Platner's campaign implode really stung, and they admit they're disappointed. Platner excited a lot of people. You know, voters saw him as a compelling candidate who was building a movement, and some aren't sure Jackson has that same ability, despite having a similar message.I met Lynn Heasley walking her dog by the harbor over in Belfast, Maine. She told me she volunteered a bunch for Platner's campaign, and though Jackson has her vote, she says the campaign shake-up sucked some of the energy out of this movement for her.LYNN HEASLEY: I'm not completely, like, done and given up. But no, I'm not as excited. That's a personality thing, and I think what's most important is whether the job gets done and whether we have people voting the way we need them to be voting.MOORE: Other Jackson supporters are still really excited, though. I talked to University of Maine PhD student and delegate Aurora Green right before she headed into the convention today.AURORA GREEN: This isn't about Graham Platner. This isn't even about Troy Jackson. This is about a movement of working-class Mainers and workers.ELLIOTT: Elena, with the convention over, the fall matchup is now set between Jackson and Republican Susan Collins. What happens next?MOORE: Yeah, I mean, make no mistake. Jackson has a long road ahead of him if he wants to unseat Collins. This is someone who has held this seat in Maine for 30 years and has a ton of campaign cash. Her campaign is already on the offensive, criticizing Jackson in a statement today for what they said was a partisan record of driving up costs. Of course, Jackson makes the exact same argument about her, and says that a grassroots movement calling for a rejection of the political establishment can stand a chance.So all eyes will be on Maine to see if Jackson can do just that because, as a reminder, the results of this race could have political implications nationwide. It's one of just a few matchups that could end up determining which party controls the Senate next year.ELLIOTT: That's NPR political reporter Elena Moore in Bangor, Maine. Thanks so much.MOORE: Happy to do it. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. articles.title: Democrats approve a new primary election calendar, putting South Carolina first
articles.summary: In this file photo, people wait to vote on the first day of early voting on May 26, 2026 in Columbia, S.C. Sean Rayford/Getty Images hide caption
articles.full_content: In this file photo, people wait to vote on the first day of early voting on May 26, 2026 in Columbia, S.C. Sean Rayford/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption Sean Rayford/Getty Images South Carolina was chosen to hold the first Democratic presidential primary in 2028 after a panel voted on the calendar Friday afternoon. The move was pushed by key Democrats to prioritize Black voters, a reliable and influential voting bloc for the party. The Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws panel recommended South Carolina vote first over Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa, who had each been seeking the first spot. Only six states will be permitted to hold primaries before Super Tuesday on March 7, 2028. The order recommended by the panel is South Carolina's primary, to be held on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada and New Hampshire, which are typically early voting states. New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia would also be permitted to hold early contests. This calendar will be presented to the full DNC in August, to be voted on and finalized. Sponsor Message South Carolina and the other five states could now hold early nominating contests, a play they have been pushing for since the start of this year. The NPR Politics Podcast 2028 fantasy draft: Democrats During the committee meeting Friday some states' party leaders and allies were making cases for why their state should go early. "The place to start is in the West," said David McDonald, a member of the committee. "The place to start is in Nevada, which offers the best combination of diversity, certainty and opportunity." McDonald was likely referring to Nevada's diverse population of Latino, Black, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Native American and working class voters. Nevada was considered alongside South Carolina because the party also wants to prioritize Latino voters, a voting group that had a significant election impact in 2024 when President Trump won reelection. Because 2028 is an open primary, advocates for these two states argue they give candidates the best chance to be tested by influential voting blocs. At the end, some members raised concerns about Nevada being able to rapidly process election results. South Carolina previously led the Democratic presidential primary in 2024 — the first time the process didn't start with the Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire's primary election. Some members of the panel spoke about the southern state's role in former President Joe Biden's 2020 nomination. Biden picked up his first early state victory in South Carolina that year, before winning other southern states on Super Tuesday. Sponsor Message Elections Democrats wanted answers for what went wrong in 2024. Now, there are more questions Politics Trump leans on 'communist' messaging as economic angst drives Democrats Nearly one in four registered voters in South Carolina is Black, according to state voting data. According to AP Vote Cast, 83% of Black voters nationwide backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in the last presidential election. "The South is not the past, we are the future," said Christale Spain, chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party. "And if we are serious about changing this country, Democrats have to start winning in the South." Spain said Democrats need to demonstrate that they are serious about making the investment in the South, adding that South Carolina has a lot of flexibility for its election dates and two weeks of early voting. South Carolina allies said that the party should show that Black voters are a priority for them in a year when the Supreme Court's Voting Rights Act decision led to multiple states drawing new congressional boundaries in districts that had previously ruled in violation of that law. The six states picked to be first together tell the story of who the Democratic Party is, said Debbie Dingell, a congresswoman from Michigan, urging members not to read too much into who was given the first slot. Michigan will also vote early in the current plan.

articles.full_content: Transcript AILSA CHANG, HOST: It's CONSIDER THIS, where every day we go deep on one big news story. Today, President Trump is doubling down on tariffs. In February, the Supreme Court struck down his sweeping tariffs. President Trump was visibly angry. The court ruled that he couldn't impose tariffs under a law called the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. During a press conference shortly after that ruling, Trump responded with this.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: But other alternatives will now be used to replace the ones that the court incorrectly rejected. We have alternatives. Great alternatives.CHANG: Alternatives as in alternative laws that the administration might use to authorize tariffs. Today, the Trump administration brought that plan to fruition by imposing a new set of tariffs on more than 80 countries.CONSIDER THIS - after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's previous tariffs, he is doubling down with new ones. What's different this time, and how could it affect the average consumer?(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)CHANG: From NPR, I'm Ailsa Chang.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)CHANG: It's CONSIDER THIS FROM NPR. President Trump's tariffs have caused an array of problems for him. They have raised prices. They've caused other countries to retaliate. And polls show that voters don't like these tariffs. Nevertheless, he has remained remarkably firm in keeping tariffs as a cornerstone of his economic agenda, imposing a new wave of tariffs on Friday. Here to tell us more are NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben and NPR senior business editor Rafael Nam. Hello to both of you.DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Hey there.RAFAEL NAM, BYLINE: Hey.CHANG: Hey. OK. Danielle, I want to start with you. Can you just tell us more about these newest tariffs? Like, what are they replacing exactly?KURTZLEBEN: Right. So these new tariffs have two tiers - 10% and 12.5%. And they cover all of the biggest U.S. trading partners, which are responsible for almost all of the imports to the U.S. Now, that said, some major categories of goods are exempted here, like energy and some types of foods.CHANG: OK.KURTZLEBEN: Now, these new tariffs will replace a temporary global 10% blanket tariff that Trump put into place right after that Supreme Court decision you mentioned. That tariff expired this week. These new tariffs took their place. Now, to impose these new tariffs, the administration is using a law intended to counter other countries', quote, "unfair trade practices." In this case, the U.S. is accusing all of its major trading partners of not doing enough to fight the use of forced labor. Now, not everyone buys that rationale. Democratic Representative Richard Neal from Massachusetts said in a statement that Trump is just hunting for legal justifications, and that the new tariffs are, quote, "too convenient to be taken seriously."CHANG: And wait. These weren't even the only tariffs that Trump imposed this week, right?KURTZLEBEN: Right. He also announced new tariffs on some specific categories of Canadian goods. Those are 50% tariffs, so they're pretty high.CHANG: Yeah.KURTZLEBEN: And they're set to take effect in just under a month. The administration said those are to retaliate against Canada's own retaliation against U.S. tariffs last year.CHANG: We're in this time when the cost of living - it's such a top concern for so many households. How do you think these tariffs will affect those households?NAM: The good news is that - if you can call it that - is that it may not - if that - is that they're not significantly higher than the tariffs they are replacing. But they are still a lot higher than they were at the start of the second Trump administration. And this has a real impact on American families, especially at a time, like you said, Ailsa, when the cost of living is a real concern. It's also that the war with Iran has led to a big increase in gas prices. The Budget Lab at Yale University says the latest tariffs will add a little under a percentage point to consumer inflation. And in dollar terms, that means an additional tax of $1,100 to households per year, actually.CHANG: Wow.NAM: All of this clearly has a knock-on effect, according to Natasha Sarin, the president of the Budget Lab. Inflation rises because of tariffs. People therefore spend less, and the end result is a hit to the economy. This is how she put it.NATASHA SARIN: You never make up that. It's sort of a permanent decline in the economy's strength as a result of this type of policy.NAM: And that's why many economists think tariffs are a really bad idea.CHANG: Well, given that tariffs are adding to people's financial problems, why go through with them?KURTZLEBEN: Well, this White House has a couple of policy reasons. First, they often use tariffs as leverage to get concessions from other countries on trade agreements. And it's possible, by the way, that that could happen with these new Canada tariffs I mentioned. Like I said, there's almost a month until they go into effect, and the U.S. and Canada still need to sit down and renegotiate the USMCA trade pact. So these tariffs could change or disappear during those negotiations.CHANG: OK.KURTZLEBEN: Now, the White House's main rationale for tariffs is that they will revitalize manufacturing. That boom has not materialized yet in jobs. In fact, there are fewer manufacturing jobs now than when Trump took office. Now, the White House has also claimed trillions of dollars in new investment as a result of trade deals stemming from his tariffs. New investment could result in more jobs. But also, the numbers have been unclear, and we still have to see when or if all of that money materializes.CHANG: Exactly. OK. So, Rafael, the administration is saying tariffs will pay off, but we're obviously living in the present moment. What kind of effects are these tariffs having right now?NAM: So besides the higher cost of living, the main thing is that it does make things unpredictable. Take the Federal Reserve. Tariffs are just another complication at a time when policymakers are grappling with higher energy costs and high borrowing costs. For example, the average 30-year mortgage just hit its highest in nearly a year. All of this could make it more likely the Fed will have to raise interest rates this year, which goes against the president, who has been arguing that the Fed should be lowering rates.But for businesses today, the effects of these tariffs are real. You've heard us say this time and time again. Businesses hate uncertainty, and right now that's what they're getting. Not only that - the president has a habit of threatening to impose additional tariffs all of a sudden. He did that with Canada earlier this week, for example.CHANG: Right.NAM: And Sarin at the Budget Lab says those kinds of sudden actions make life extremely tough for businesses.SARIN: And so I think that makes it, like, really challenging from the perspective of businesses who are trying to plan to understand, like, what their costs are going to be and also then what prices they're going to have to charge consumers for these goods if you don't have any real sense of the ways in which the policy is evolving.NAM: So Trump may be arguing tariffs will pay off. But businesses, though, are not feeling it right now.CHANG: But - OK. Danielle, just make this make sense. Like, how do these tariffs make sense politically with midterm elections approaching?KURTZLEBEN: Well, that's really a gamble, I think. Trump's pro-tariff argument is essentially, I'm using these now to make great deals. They can bring in some revenue, but the biggest economic effects will show up eventually. Now, some voters may buy into that long-term narrative, but polls have shown that tariffs have grown less and less popular. And that, along with higher gas prices from the Iran war, has dragged the president's approval down.Now, if you're a Republican running this November, you have a tough question. Do you try to create daylight between yourself and Trump on tariffs? And if you do, how do voters react and how does the president react? Both of those things are very unpredictable.CHANG: That is NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben and Rafael Nam. Thank you to both of you.KURTZLEBEN: Yeah. Thank you.NAM: Thank you.CHANG: This episode was produced by Michelle Aslam and Karen Zamora, with audio engineering by Ted Mebane. Our director is Jonas Adams. articles.title: How The Illharmonic's mix of hip-hop and classical builds community, one show at a time
articles.summary: Kaleb Cabell, Andrea Coln McNeill and Jeffrey McNeill perform as part of The Illharmonic Orchestra at NPR's Washington headquarters. Brianna Scott/NPR hide caption
articles.full_content: Kaleb Cabell, Andrea Coln McNeill and Jeffrey McNeill perform as part of The Illharmonic Orchestra at NPR's Washington headquarters. Brianna Scott/NPR hide caption toggle caption Brianna Scott/NPR Vocalist and composer Jeffrey McNeill says it was back in 1987, when he was still a kid, when he first started hearing the links between hip-hop and classical music. "I was put in flute and piano lessons as a child, and my father introduced me to The Sugarhill Gang, 'Rapper's Delight,'" McNeill explained in an interview with All Things Considered. "One day, my brother brought home the Beastie Boys' 'Paul Revere,' and to me, it sounded like it went perfectly with Beethoven's 5th Symphony." Nearly 40 years later, the marriage of those two genres — as well as McNeill's literal marriage to fellow artist Andrea Coln McNeill — are manifest in The Illharmonic Orchestra, which has booked shows in major concert venues across the country over the last two decades. Sponsor Message McNeill — who performs as "Thee Phantom" — and Coln McNeill — who is also known as "The Phoenix" — blend hip-hop and R&B vocals with live horns, woodwinds, strings and percussion, performed by all-Black orchestral ensembles. That representation in classical music performance is a key goal for the group's leaders. "It was really important for us to show that these two genres are not as completely different as people think they are," Coln McNeill told NPR's Juana Summers during a visit to NPR headquarters. "Even in 2026, some of the major symphony orchestras still are really lacking in diversity. But there's clearly a reflection that those individuals exist. We play with them all the time," she explained. "Folks who look like us, who play these instruments, who have the training, who have been to the conservatory, who have the Ph.D.s, or self-taught — we know that that talent level exists within the folks that look like us." And for many of their audiences, the experience can be transformative, said McNeill — on top of being a lot of fun. "It's a house party in a concert hall. It's a community experience," he said. "And it has helped the performances so much that the people actually get it, and they connect with the music and they connect with us, and they see us on stage and they see themselves in us on stage. And that's really kind of what's kept us going for this long." Sponsor Message Ahead of a performance at the Lincoln Theater in Washington, D.C., The Illharmonic Orchestra stopped by NPR to offer a special performance. Listen to the full interview and their performance by clicking on the blue button above, and you can find their performance schedule here. Audio for this performance chat was engineered by Andie Huether and Tiffany Vera Castro. The performers with The Illharmonic Orchestra at NPR were: Andrea Coln McNeill Vocalist Jeffrey McNeill - Vocalist Tauhida Smith - Violin Leanne Holmes - Violin Jillian Uzuegbu - Violin Tara Cuffee - Viola Kaleb Cabell - Cello Robert Chittams - Bass Alissa Gittens - Flute/Piccolo Ronnal Ford - Saxophone/Flute Xavier Hendon - Trumpet Robert McIver - Trumpet Tim Johnson - Trombone Ashlei Peoples - Keyboards

articles.full_content: Transcript JUANA SUMMERS, HOST: Some of my favorite stories that I've reported have come together by chance. I was scrolling through videos on social media when I found a short clip from an orchestra performing hip-hop music.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)SUMMERS: It's the Illharmonic Orchestra, a Philadelphia-based group fronted by a husband and wife duo who go by the stage names the Phantom and the Phoenix. And I had to know more about them. So I invited Jeffrey McNeill - he's the Phantom - and Andrea Coln McNeill, aka the Phoenix, here to NPR headquarters in Washington earlier this summer. Their chemistry instantly lit up the studio. You can feel it in how they perform, even in the way they take cues from each other.ANDREA COLN MCNEILL: Oh, are you waiting on me?(LAUGHTER)SUMMERS: And they brought along some of the local musicians they've been working with for years...(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)JEFFREY MCNEILL: (Rapping) Send them some mic magnificent most auspicious...SUMMERS: ...An all-Black orchestral ensemble. I started by asking Jeffrey and Andrea to tell us what it feels like when the Illharmonic Orchestra performs live in front of big crowds. And I'll let Jeffrey pick it up from here.MCNEILL: It's a house party in a concert hall. It is a community experience. When we perform, we invite the audience sort of into the performance. You know, we encourage them to sing along and dance along and just really be a part of the experience.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)COLN MCNEILL: (Rapping) Me and the Phantom, yo, we blowing the spot 'cause we're a double...MCNEILL: (Rapping) Double.COLN MCNEILL: (Rapping)...Trouble, and we're bubbling hot.MCNEILL: Yeah.SUMMERS: Can you talk a little bit about some of the challenges of bringing hip-hop into the classical space, but also helping Black people feel like this is a space for us where we can thrive and belong?COLN MCNEILL: Well, that's something that we struggled with very early in our inception of the Illharmonic, was really the naysayers around putting these two genres together.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) Put your hands together for hip-hop. Put your hands together.COLN MCNEILL: (Inaudible).So it was really important for us to show that these two genres are not as completely different as people think they are. Another thing that was really important about us putting together the Illharmonic is us wanting to see reflected in classical music, which we love tremendously, things that we don't see reflected on a regular basis when we go to a classical performance.SUMMERS: Give me some examples of that.COLN MCNEILL: Even in 2026, some of the major symphony orchestras still are really lacking in diversity and being able to see that. But there's clearly a reflection that those individuals exist. We play with them all the time.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) See my name in bright lights on the worldwide tour. Spit fire through this mic and let it fall to the floor and step off while the crowd screaming...COLN MCNEILL: (Rapping) Give us some more.MCNEILL: (Rapping) Somewhere...COLN MCNEILL: So we know that those folks who look like us, who play these instruments, who have the training, who have been to the conservatory, who have, you know, the Ph.D.s and then some or self taught - we know that that talent level exists within the folks that look like us. So putting this together and making sure that we're extremely intentional about what we're showcasing is paramount for us and very important.SUMMERS: Tell us about "Sweet Dreams."(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)COLN MCNEILL: Dream, dream.MARTIN LUTHER KING JR: I have a dream.MCNEILL: It features a piece of Dr. Martin Luther King's I Have a Dream speech. It was a very pivotal moment when I wrote the third verse. It was in the wake of the Trayvon Martin verdict.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) Dream that I can reach the kids of the day. Give them all a dream, like MLK.And it really felt like a moment that I felt like I needed to say something. And it's a very relevant message to today, you know, so many years later.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) Black president two terms. And it still don't stop till the moment you could chill on top. Dream of the day you could walk down the block with Skittles and an Icee and not get shot.SUMMERS: At this point, you all have performed in all kinds of venues, from the Kennedy Center here in Washington, D.C., to Carnegie Hall. That is incredible.MCNEILL: We were getting rejection letters on the regular from Carnegie Hall until one day, I just asked, you know, how much does it cost to rent you? And then, you know, we were provided the information, and we put together a kickstarter and, you know, put together 25 musicians of our own to put on that stage. And the light bulb moment for me was watching people walk into that space and looking around in amazement and wonderment at (crying) seeing their family on the stage that they never thought they would. You know, so for us, you know, that's what's kept us going this long. And, you know, we appreciate being able to share those opportunities with others.SUMMERS: Yeah. Is there a moment or a memory that you can share that sticks in your mind that shows the power of what you've built and what the Illharmonic Orchestra has meant to people?COLN MCNEILL: One that's very near and dear to us, very special to us - in 2017, the Illharmonic performed at the Kennedy Center for New Year's Eve, and a young woman approached us with her son - at the time he was 10 - and she said to us, I just wanted to tell you what this show meant to me. And I want you to know that my son plays the cello, and I needed him to see himself reflected on stage. I needed him to see Black excellence personified and let him know that he can do this, too. And fast forward to 2026, you know, he's played in upwards of seven shows with us now. It's a full circle moment that we could have never, ever, ever anticipated.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) It all started when this man was a youth, sung in the choir, took lessons on piano and flute.SUMMERS: Kaleb Cabell, I want to bring you in now. Andrea has been bragging on you a little bit. What is it like now performing with the Illarmonic Orchestra?KALEB CABELL: Working to earn that opportunity meant so much and finally being able to achieve it after what felt like so long and kind of just keeping that memory with me through every one of my challenges and experiences going through life, it was like, hold on. Time is coming. And it was really, really inspirational.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) The kid stuck to it. Bro became fluent...SUMMERS: Tell us about the song "The Entertainer."MCNEILL: It's Kaleb's favorite. It's a song I wrote with another Black composer by the name of Jonathan Bingham. It actually started as a voice memo on my phone and has grown to a song that has incorporated about 50 different instruments on stage.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MCNEILL: (Rapping) I do not seek fortune or fame.SUMMERS: Kaleb, what do you hope to inspire in the people who come out to see you, your fellow musicians, the Illharmonic Orchestra play in venues all across the country?CABELL: I hope to show them the same thing that these guys have shown to me. I want people to realize that it's not impossible that a lot of your dreams, a lot of your hopes, a lot of your desires, they are within your reach. And I feel like the bond that I share with the people in this community is something that is really going to affect me the rest of my life.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)SUMMERS: Jeffrey and Andrea, I want to bring it back to you. What does it mean to you to be back here performing in Washington again?MCNEILL: We're always excited to come back to D.C., Chocolate City, and perform. The audience always gives us a lot of energy.COLN MCNEILL: And I think that, you know, even in today's climate of, you know, what things look like now, while folks are trying to erase our place in this country, what we've contributed to this country, what we continue to try to do and push forward in this representation is just as important now as it was 26 years ago.SUMMERS: We've been speaking with Jeffrey and Andrea McNeill and Kaleb Cabell of the Illharmonic Ochestra. Thanks to all of you.MCNEILL: Thank you.CABELL: Thank you so much.COLN MCNEILL: Thank you, Juana.SUMMERS: The Illharmonic Orchestra's performance schedule continues in cities across the country through October. In Kenya and Nigeria, economics isn't just theory, it's real life. We'll look at some radical experiments that turned out to be enormously successful. What are the building blocks of health, education and prosperity for all? How does a nation grow rich? What is the most effective way to spend a dollar to fight poverty? Really?SURI: Not everybody 100%, but voter turnout rates are extremely high. And as you can imagine, people stand in line for hours and hours on end to vote.SMITH: That enthusiasm is similar to how everyone seems to have their own business. People like to get involved in the civic and business life of the country.SURI: I think in general, that's one thing that's true, is everybody wants to participate in the economy. Think of even young people, as I said, right? They're not getting into a university, and they're frustrated because they want to participate in the economy. The entrepreneurship piece we saw-- there's this sort of wanting to participate in the social and economic life in a very deep way, I think. And that's through voting in politics. You see it in that entrepreneurial spirit we talked about. So that piece I find very inspiring, and I think it's up to us to figure out how to deliver on that, right?SMITH: I think that's a good mission statement for economists everywhere. Tavneet, there will be a test at the end of this semester of Summer School. Maybe you could help us with defining some of the concepts from today's episode.SURI: Sure, with one caveat-- I don't have to do any of the grading.SMITH: No, it's all automatic.SURI: [CHUCKLES]SMITH: Everybody passes.SURI: Oh, great.SMITH: OK. What is this randomized controlled trial-- I should say, Nobel Prize-winning randomized controlled trial-- that everyone's talking about?SURI: A randomized controlled trial is a way of studying the impact of something where you basically split a population, a study population, into two groups randomly, and one group gets the intervention and one doesn't. It allows you to sort of estimate the impact of that program very cleanly.SMITH: A lot of the randomized controlled trials we talked about in this episode involved human capital. What is human capital?SURI: Human capital is education and health. So think of it as the capital embodied in our-- in humans, in people.SMITH: It's investing in humans, instead of investing in money, although it does cost money.SURI: Correct.SMITH: Yes.SURI: It does cost a lot of money.SMITH: Finally, we talked about the missing middle as a problem faced by businesses in countries in Africa. What is the missing middle?SURI: So the missing middle is where I don't have businesses that are middle-sized in terms of their employees. I have lots of very small businesses with, you know, one or two employees. I have a bunch of big businesses that are in the hundreds of employees, but I'm missing this middle set of business that have kind of 5, 10, 15, 20 employees.[MUSIC PLAYING]SMITH: Tavneet Suri from the MIT Sloan School of Management, thank you so much for coming in, for talking with us.SURI: You're very welcome. It's been a pleasure. I had fun talking with you, too.SMITH: When are you next going to Kenya? Your parents want to know.SURI: August.SMITH: Nice. As you travel with us around the world for Summer School, you might want to bring along a guidebook to the economy. Luckily, we wrote one-- Planet Money A Guide to the Economic Forces That Shape Your Life. It's like a podcast, but with beautiful, full-color illustrations. It's always in my carry-on. And, hey, if you have lived in some country with a smart economic idea the rest of the world should know about, please tell us, and you might be featured in our graduation episode. Perhaps, you know a different way to do taxes, a mega project that came in under budget, somewhere where rent is cheap-- huh? Get in touch, now. Email us at planetmoney@npr.org, and put Summer School in the subject. Summer School is produced by Sophia Paliza-Carre and edited by Alex Goldmark. It's fact-checked by Leyla Doss. This show was engineered by Annlie Huang. I'm Robert Smith. When I'm not summer schooling, I'm also the host of the new podcast, Business History. It's a show about the history of business. This is NPR. Thanks for listening.[ANNOUNCEMENT CHIME]ANNOUNCER: We have now started boarding our Planet Money flight. articles.full_content: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories The House yesterday approved a resolution to remove U.S. forces from the war in Iran as the conflict continues to escalate in the Middle East. The non-binding resolution reflects lawmakers' disapproval of a war they did not vote to authorize. It marked the second such rebuke passed by the House since the war began. Soon after the House vote, Senate Democrats attempted to advance their own war powers resolution, but it failed 47 to 49. In the past two weeks of renewed fighting, the U.S. has launched strikes on Iran, while Iran has targeted American bases in the Gulf and Jordan, impacting global energy markets. The U.S. Capitol is seen from the Cannon House Office Building on July 22. J. Scott Applewhite/AP hide caption toggle caption J. Scott Applewhite/AP 🎧 Brent crude oil reached its highest level since May yesterday when it surged more than 6% to $100 a barrel, NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi tells Up First. The spike will impact everyday people, increasing costs for school supplies and fresh food. Shipping companies like UPS are tacking on fuel surcharges. Prices rose after Iran-backed Yemeni Houthis attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they got involved in the war to retaliate against Saudi Arabia for its siege on Yemen and assaults on the capital's international airport. Earlier this week, the rebel group also threatened to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The strait is another crucial chokepoint for oil and fuel transport, in addition to the Strait of Hormuz, which the U.S. and Iran have been fighting for control over. The ongoing conflict has also led some foreign missions to reduce their presence in Iran, according to Al-Shalchi. Sponsor Message The Trump administration announced overnight that it is imposing tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union. The new tariffs have two tiers — 10% and 12.5% — and went into effect at midnight, at the same time as when a 10% global tariff struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year expired. The administration said it imposed these new tariffs because these countries are importing goods made with forced labor. The tariffs cover more than 99% of imports to the United States. Major categories like energy and many foods will remain exempt. Earlier this week, President Trump also signed proclamations to impose 50% tariffs on a selection of Canadian goods. 🎧 Polls show that Americans largely disapprove of tariffs and that their approval of Trump's handling of the economy has declined, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. Despite public opinion, she says Trump views tariffs as a tool to pressure other countries into making concessions on things like trade deals. As the midterm elections approach, the administration continues to assert that its tariff policies will yield long-term economic benefits. Some economists caution that it is risky to ask voters to back a potentially unpopular approach, given the uncertainty of future outcomes. A vigil last night in Madison, Wisconsin, drew hundreds of people mourning 38-year-old Corey Ruiz, a man shot and killed by police on Wednesday. Madison Police Chief John Patterson said that officers responded to a call about a man checking cars. When they arrived, Ruiz fled on his bike. When officers attempted to arrest him, he produced a knife and injured one officer, according to the police chief. Four officers were involved in the incident. The officer who was injured was the one who shot Ruiz. Authorities have not yet released his name. The four officers have been placed on administrative leave. Sponsor Message 🎧 Emotions are running high in the city since the shooting, says Sarah Lehr of NPR network station Wisconsin Public Radio. The community is particularly raw to this incident, having experienced two other deadly shootings by police in the same neighborhood since 2012, Lehr adds. The Wisconsin Division of Criminal Investigation is looking into the shooting. The officers involved in the incident were not wearing body cameras, as the Madison police don't have them department-wide. Madison police do have dashboard cameras, and there are multiple bystander videos circulating of the incident, Lehr says. Living better Research into any health benefits of avocado oil lags behind the studies of other oils, such as olive and seed oils. fcafotodigital/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption fcafotodigital/Getty Images Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America. A growing number of consumers are interested in avocado oil's purported health benefits. But some people might not be getting what they think they're buying. A new study finds that consumers paying a premium for foods advertised as containing avocado oil are probably not receiving it, highlighting ongoing authenticity issues in the industry. Selina Wang, the lead author of the study, says the findings are particularly disheartening, as avocado oil products are often much more expensive than those made with olive or other vegetable oils. Here's what we know: 🥑 In a study, researchers conducted a chemical analysis of 54 products that listed only avocado oil. They found that 89% were adulterated with cheaper oils like soybean.🥑 In comparison, researchers found that, out of 20 packaged foods made with olive oil tested, only one showed signs of adulteration.🥑 Some see avocado oil as a healthier alternative to seed oils like canola and soybean. According to Sarah Berry, a nutrition professor at King's College London, there's limited direct evidence supporting its health benefits compared to data about eating avocados.🥑 Avocado oil costs more largely because avocados are costly and produce a limited amount of oil. Catch the film adaptation of Hadestown: The Musical, a retelling of the Greek tragedy of Orpheus and Eurydice. The show is in theaters for a limited time. Sponsor Message 📺 TV: Netflix's new series The Hawk stars Will Ferrell as a past-his-prime golfer. In the show, he reunites with some former collaborators, including Molly Shannon, Luke Wilson and Chris Parnell. 📚 Books: Grace Farris' graphic memoir See One, Do One, Teach One gives readers an insider's look at medical school, including the stresses of student loans, friendships built under pressure and the impossible pursuit of work-life balance. 🎵 Music: NPR's New Music Friday is breaking down the best new albums out today, and Charli xcx, Tyla and Shania Twain are on that list. Check out the other albums that made the cut and listen to a playlist of new songs. 🕹️ Gaming: Discover the best games of 2026 so far as NPR staff members spotlight some of their favorites with this interactive list. ❓Quiz: This week's quiz features a variety of topics, from a deformed yet adorable animal to international politics. Sterling, Ky. in April. AFP via Getty Images hide caption toggle caption AFP via Getty Images AMMAN, Jordan — The U.S. continued airstrikes in Iran on Friday while Tehran launched retaliatory attacks on U.S. targets in the Gulf as the region braced itself after President Trump said he was close to deciding whether to launch the biggest offensive of the war. "I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision," Trump told the Axios news outlet. Middle East U.S.-Iran strikes escalate as the ongoing war rattles global energy markets The U.S. military later said it conducted its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran in attacks aimed at degrading Iran's ability to threaten maritime traffic. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was quoted by state media as saying "Iran has shown that it will not bow to U.S. bullying and will under no circumstances respond to the language of force, pressure and threats." He also said he had "detailed" talks with the foreign ministers of Russia and China. Sponsor Message The standoff continues over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway between Iran and Oman, with Iran asserting its control and the U.S. imposing a blockade on Iranian ports. The conflict on Thursday pushed global benchmark oil prices to over $100 per barrel, their highest level since May. The price has since fallen below $92 a barrel Friday. The national average price for regular gasoline in the U.S. continued to climb to $4.10 per gallon — up more than 17 cents from a month ago, according to AAA. Loading... Iranian state media reported explosions overnight, including along the Strait of Hormuz in Qeshm and Bandar Abbas. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres told the U.N. Security Council that the Middle East was "teetering on the edge of [the] unimaginable." Politics For a 2nd time, House approves resolution to end the war in Iran in a rebuke to Trump "The situation is getting out of control," Guterres said. "The region is being pulled into an ever-widening circle of confrontation. One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next." The collapse of the ceasefire has brought Yemen's Houthi rebels, a key Iranian ally, further into the conflict. The Houthis this week attacked Saudi tankers in the Red Sea near Bab el-Mandeb. The Houthis control that waterway, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is vital to global container traffic moving through the Suez Canal. Middle East conflict U.S. and Iranian attacks continue as tensions mount on a key waterway in the Red Sea Trump threatened "major military punishment" against the Houthis if the attacks continue. Saudi Arabia backs an internationally recognized Yemeni government that controls the north of Yemen. The Houthis blame Saudi Arabia for an attack on the airport in the Yemeni capital last week. In the Kurdistan region of Iraq, security forces shot down explosive-laden drones near the regional capital Irbil's international airport. The airport director said it had closed temporarily but was operating normally again later Friday morning. Smoke rises after explosions were heard and air defenses activated near the airport in Irbil, in the Kurdistan region of northern Iraq, on Friday. Several blasts sounded near the Irbil airport, which hosts U.S.-led coalition troops, an AFP journalist said. AFP via Getty Images hide caption toggle caption AFP via Getty Images Iran did not issue claims of responsibility for the strikes in the Iraqi Kurdish region where the U.S. has a military presence. Armed Kurdish-Iranian opposition bases in the Kurdish region have been a frequent target of Iranian and Iranian-backed attacks. Sponsor Message Newly appointed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said after a visit Thursday to Iran he had promised not to allow attacks on Iran from Iraqi soil. Zaidi met President Trump this week in Washington, where he promised to intensify efforts to rein in Iran-backed Iraqi militias that have attacked U.S. forces. In response to the increased tension, the United Kingdom announced it was temporarily withdrawing diplomatic staff from Iran. Some airlines began canceling flights to the region. Qatar Airways, a major regional carrier, announced it would suspend flights to Bahrain, Kuwait and Irbil until the end of July.

articles.title: Netflix viewers the world over are binge-watching South African series 'The Polygamist.' Here's why
articles.summary: The Polygamist. Gugu Gumede as Joyce Gomora in The Polygamist. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026 Mpumelelo Macu/Netflix hide caption
articles.full_content: The Polygamist. Gugu Gumede as Joyce Gomora in The Polygamist. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026 Mpumelelo Macu/Netflix hide caption toggle caption Mpumelelo Macu/Netflix JOHANNESBURG, South Africa—Netflix's The Polygamist, a Zulu-language telenovela, has become a national talking point in South Africa. But the scandal-filled saga has also emerged as a surprise global hit, with audiences from Romania to Hong Kong to the U.S. bingeing the twists, betrayals and family drama. The story of a cheating husband's double life racked up more than 23 million views in its first month, reaching the top ten in 62 countries, including the US, and the number one spot in almost two dozen countries. The Polygamist, set in Johannesburg, centers on a wealthy Black family, the Gomoras, and follows the matriarch Joyce as she tries to keep up appearances as her businessman husband Jonasi sets up house with another woman. Sponsor Message Over the course of the 22 episodes vicious catfights break out, homes are set alight, there's a lot of sex and swearing, and all the incredible twists and turns are enough to give the viewer whiplash. Even celebrities have been taking to social media to rave about the series, including former host of The View, Sherri Shepard. "I'm about to go back and finish watching The Polygamist because I'm hooked now," she said on her Instagram account. "Crazy rich Africans, I thought Crazy Rich Asians was something, but crazy rich Africans is a whole other level. Good grief! What?!" Shepard continued, referring to the hit 2018 romantic-comedy set among wealthy Singaporeans. The Polygamist. (L to R) Sdumo Mtshali as Jonasi Gomora, Kwanele Mthethewa as Matipa in The Polygamist. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026 Netflix hide caption toggle caption Netflix Sue Nyathi, the Zimbabwean writer who wrote the book the show was based on, says she thinks this is exactly one of the reasons foreign viewers are amazed by the show. "It also showcases a different kind of African lifestyle that viewers are not familiar with, you know, the rich African…because oftentimes in media, we have one lens in which Africans are viewed," she says. "It's always the poor struggling Africans. And this is not to dismiss the poverty in Africa. No, but it's also saying that there is also a society of Africans that are very, you know, affluent, well off." Sponsor Message And it's not quiet luxury. The scenes are set in gilded Johannesburg mansions with lush gardens, and there are high-end vehicles and designer clothes aplenty. But Nyathi says she also thinks the story transcends borders because "It's a series that holds up a mirror to society and people see themselves in one form or the other. And so because it resonates deeply, that's what makes it popular." "I mean, as much as Jonas is a polygamist, he's also a cheating husband. Infidelity, things of infidelity permeate the story. And I think that's a problem that is universal, you know," she adds. "You have a married couple, then you have the mistress or the paramour, the side chick, whatever you want to call it. And that story is familiar for a lot of people." A Zimbabwean writer and a President's daughter Nyathi says her book struggled to gain traction when first published, so the Netflix adaptation has been a huge boost, with the novel now flying off the shelves in South Africa. Even people who are not regular readers have told her at book signings they were keen to buy her novel. Nyathi says she was inspired to write the book after seeing how African men were deviating from traditional open polygamy, to having secret second families, and the negative effects this was having on the women. "So in the book, the story is told from the women's POV (point of view). The man never speaks…Because we've heard men speak all our lives. And men will always justify why they want to have more than one wife." "I wanted to give the women a voice as to say, why would they choose this kind of setup, you know," Nyathi added. Sue Nyathi, writer of the book "The Polygamist" with Gugu Zuma-Ncube, one of the producers of the Netflix series by the same name. Courtesy of Sue Nyathi hide caption toggle caption Courtesy of Sue Nyathi In South Africa, polygamy is allowed under traditional law –- but not civil law. In its traditional form it is not secret, with all the wives knowing about one another. The Zulu monarchs practice polygamy, and the current King has three wives -- with a scandal erupted earlier this month over one of them. Sponsor Message King Misuzulu kaZwelithini was seen in a leaked video threatening to physically assault Queen Nomzamo Myeni, who he said had taken a lover. He berated her, then ordered her to leave his household. It's a topic the Netflix series producers know all about. It's made by Gugu Zuma-Ncube and Thuli Zuma, two of the daughters of the country's most high-profile polygamist – former President Jacob Zuma, who has four wives. "My father is a polygamist. He had several wives…it's definitely formed part of my experience. It's formed a big chunk of my childhood, just understanding the dynamics, being frustrated sometimes by a lot of it, but also trying to appreciate it for what it is and for the choices that people make," Zuma-Ncube says. Her Dad hasn't watched the show yet, but she thinks he will eventually. "I'm very interested to see what he thinks," she says. Zuma-Ncube also hopes the show's popularity internationally will have a knock-on effect. "We were completely surprised by, completely blown away, still kind of pinching ourselves at the moment, as to how well it's done abroad," she said. "I think the attention that it's gotten, the welcome and reception that it's gotten, I think will help the entire industry and will benefit all African storytellers." The show is in the Zulu language, though it moves seamlessly between English and other languages too – which mirrors South Africa's fully multilingual reality. The Polygamist. (L to R) Noluthando Shabalala as Mpume Gomora, Kwanele Mthethewa as Matipa, S'dumo Mtshali as Jonasi Gomora in The Polygamist. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026 Netflix hide caption toggle caption Netflix But it also has a dubbed version, which is voiced by South Africans and keeps some of the local vernacular. Foreign viewers will be introduced to common words like "haibo!' an exclamation meaning 'wow!,' and the South Africa-wide weekend institution of "braaiing" or barbecuing. But Zuma-Ncube encourages viewer to give the original audio with subtitles a try, noting "I was watching a creator from (South) Korea who was saying she was learning how to speak Zulu watching the show, which was really, really interesting." Sponsor Message And the show has been igniting debate in South Africa too, not just about polygamy, but about women's rights, safe sex and HIV. UNAIDS has run ads with a photo of the show's title character, saying "Don't be a Jonasi. Keep yourself and your partners safe." And a government department in South Africa's rural Limpopo province has waged an educational campaign against gender-based violence with the tagline: "The Polygamist shows fiction, Gender-based Violence and Femicide shows consequences. Break the cycle." A show built on secrets and scandal is now driving some very real conversations.

articles.summary: A reclining protestor covers himself with a banner printed with a portrait of Sonam Wangchuk, a prominent activist who was forcefully transferred to a hospital by the police as he staged a hunger strike in support of a movement led by Cockroach Janta Party, at a protest in New Delhi, India, Wednesday, July 22, 2026.
